title: Capstone Schema: Customers, Orders and Order Items
learningObjectives: Model customers, orders and order items as related entities.
Create foreign keys for customer, order and product relationships.
Explain why order items store the unit price at the time of sale.
Use CHECK constraints for positive quantities and non-negative prices.
Calculate an order total from quantity multiplied by unit price.

understand.concept: An order belongs to a customer, and an order can contain multiple order items. Each order item references a product and stores the quantity and sale-time unit price. Keeping order items separate supports multi-product orders and preserves the price charged at the time of sale.
understand.whyItMatters: A normalized order model supports accurate receipts, reporting and stock movements without storing multiple products in one order row.
understand.analogy: A database capstone is like a complete shop workflow: records, rules, operations and reports must all work together.
understand.analogyLimit: The analogy does not model database isolation, concurrent workloads, deployment security or recovery guarantees.

explain.narrative:
## Customer and order entities
A customer can place many orders. Each order references one customer. An order item belongs to one order and references one product.

## Preserve sale-time values
Store the unit price charged on the order item. Product catalogue prices can change later; historical orders should continue to show the price agreed at purchase time.

## Integrity rules
Use foreign keys for customer, order and product relationships. Use CHECK(quantity > 0) and CHECK(unit_price >= 0). Enable SQLite foreign-key enforcement for the connection when testing these rules.

### Relationship and history design
The schema uses separate customer, order-header and order-item entities to avoid repeating customer and order attributes on every line. `unit_price` belongs on the order item because it records the agreed price at the time of sale, not necessarily the current product price.

### Portability and safety
`INSERT OR IGNORE` is SQLite-specific. Prefer explicit conflict targets or carefully handled constraint errors when porting to another engine. Verify the affected-row count for seed operations and enable SQLite foreign-key enforcement before testing invalid references.

examples.title: Ensure category and product tables exist
examples.code: CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS cap19_categories (category_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, category_name TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE); CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS cap19_products (product_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, category_id INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES cap19_categories(category_id), product_name TEXT NOT NULL, unit_price REAL NOT NULL CHECK (unit_price >= 0), stock_qty INTEGER NOT NULL CHECK (stock_qty >= 0));
examples.explanation: Creates the category and product parent tables only when they do not already exist. IF NOT EXISTS avoids an already-exists error, but it does not compare an existing table's definition with the requested definition; schema migrations should inspect and validate the actual columns and constraints.

examples.title: Ensure sample products exist
examples.code: INSERT OR IGNORE INTO cap19_categories VALUES (1, 'Accessories'), (2, 'Stationery'); INSERT OR IGNORE INTO cap19_products VALUES (1, 1, 'USB Cable', 250, 20), (2, 1, 'Phone Case', 400, 12), (3, 2, 'Notebook', 60, 50);
examples.explanation: Seeds category and product rows using SQLite's INSERT OR IGNORE form. It can suppress more than duplicate-key conflicts, including other constraint violations, so it should not be used as a blanket error handler in production imports. The referenced category rows are inserted before products.

examples.title: Create customers, orders and order items
examples.code: CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS cap19_customers (customer_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, customer_name TEXT NOT NULL, phone TEXT UNIQUE); CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS cap19_orders (order_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, customer_id INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES cap19_customers(customer_id), order_date TEXT NOT NULL, order_status TEXT NOT NULL); CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS cap19_order_items (order_item_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, order_id INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES cap19_orders(order_id), product_id INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES cap19_products(product_id), quantity INTEGER NOT NULL CHECK (quantity > 0), unit_price REAL NOT NULL CHECK (unit_price >= 0));
examples.explanation: Creates three related tables. A customer can own many orders; each order can contain many order items; each order item references one product. CHECK constraints require positive quantities and non-negative sale-time unit prices. Foreign-key enforcement must be enabled on the SQLite connection.

examples.title: Insert a customer and an order
examples.code: INSERT OR IGNORE INTO cap19_customers VALUES (1, 'Asha', '9000000001'); INSERT OR IGNORE INTO cap19_orders VALUES (1, 1, '2026-11-22', 'created');
examples.explanation: Inserts a customer before the order that references customer_id 1. INSERT OR IGNORE makes this seed repeatable for this sample key, but an ignored row should be checked rather than assumed to contain the intended values.

examples.title: Add order items and calculate the order total
examples.code: INSERT OR IGNORE INTO cap19_order_items VALUES (1, 1, 1, 2, 250), (2, 1, 3, 3, 60); SELECT order_id, SUM(quantity * unit_price) AS order_total FROM cap19_order_items GROUP BY order_id;
examples.explanation: Inserts two order items and calculates the order total by summing quantity multiplied by the unit price captured on each item. The result is 2 × 250 + 3 × 60 = 680. Storing the sale-time unit price preserves historical order value if the catalogue price later changes.

practise.guidedTask: Run the examples after SQL19.1's product tables are available. Trace the customer-to-order-to-order-item relationships and calculate the receipt total.
practise.independentTask: Extend the capstone with a payment table. Decide whether an order can have multiple payments and design the keys and constraints accordingly.
hints: One customer can have many orders.
One order can have many order items.
Each order item references one product.
Store the sale-time unit price in the order item.
Calculate line totals as quantity multiplied by unit_price.

questions.prompt: What does an order item represent?
options: One product line within an order
questions.answer: One product line within an order
questions.explanation: An order item stores one product and quantity within an order.

questions.prompt: Why store unit_price on the order item?
options: To preserve the price charged when the sale occurred
To overwrite the product catalogue price
questions.answer: To preserve the price charged when the sale occurred
questions.explanation: Historical order values should not change when catalogue prices change.

questions.prompt: Which key links an order to its customer?
questions.explanation: The order references the customer who placed it.

options: Each order item has a positive quantity
questions.answer: Each order item has a positive quantity
questions.explanation: The check constraint rejects zero or negative quantities.

questions.prompt: How is an order total calculated from line items?
questions.explanation: The total is the sum of each line's quantity multiplied by its sale-time unit price.
